requirement:
A named item's `name_span` is `Some` with the span to highlight for its name
in the original source snapshot. The highlighted text may differ from the
name in the selector. Use `selector` to address the item. The file root and
anonymous items have `name_span` set to `None`. `OutlineItem::new` starts with
`None`. Language providers use `with_name_span` to set the highlight within
the item’s own span.
rationale:
structural: The structural clauses are the `name_span` field being an `Option` of a span, `OutlineItem::new` starting with `None`, and `with_name_span` as the setter that stores `Some(span)`. The other clauses are behavioral: which items get `Some` or `None`, and what the highlight covers. They are enforced and tested elsewhere, for example by `validate_outline` and the `provider_name_spans_match_selector_kind_and_item_boundaries` test. Both clauses that are structural are covered by the supplied roots.

- `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/contents.rs#impl[OutlineItem]/fn[new]` initializes `name_span: None`. An alternative that starts with `Some` would violate the clause "`OutlineItem::new` starts with `None`".
- `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/contents.rs#impl[OutlineItem]/fn[with_name_span]` sets `self.name_span = Some(span)` and returns `self`. It is the named setter the text prescribes.
- The `name_span: Option<Span>` field on `struct[OutlineItem]` is reached from `new` through the type it constructs, so it needs no separate root.

The sentence "Language providers use `with_name_span`" describes how the setter is meant to be used. It does not prescribe a build constraint. In `impl[Outline]#2/fn[from_legacy]`, the conversion assigns `item.name_span = node.name_span` directly. That gives the same observable result, so I treat the setter as the available API and not as a mandated call path.

behavioral: The reviewed tests cover each observable obligation in `requirements.sdk.outlines.name_span`.

- **`OutlineItem::new` starts with `None`.** `tests/outline_content.rs#fn[outline_constructors_preserve_fields_and_replace_attachments]` asserts `item.name_span == None` right after `new`.
- **`with_name_span` sets the highlight.** The same test calls `.with_name_span(Span::new(7, 8))` and asserts `Some(Span::new(7, 8))` on the cloned outline's item.
- **Named items get `Some(span)` in the original source, and the text may differ from the selector.** `fn[rust_name_spans_highlight_spelling_in_the_original_source]` checks the highlighted source slices:
  - `Trait for Wrapper<T>` for a selector `impl[Wrapper<T>/Trait]`.
  - `café`, a non-ASCII name.
  - `"C"` for `extern[Rust]`.
  - `fn[language_name_spans_retain_original_bytes_when_selectors_are_normalized]` does the same for other languages. It checks that Python keeps `Café`, CSS keeps `screen   and (color)` and `.a,  .b`, TOML keeps `'c/d'`, and Markdown keeps `Café   title`. It also checks that duplicate TypeScript `f` items get distinct spans.
- **The file root and anonymous items have `None`.**
  - The Rust test checks `None` for the root (`""` kind) and for the `use` item.
  - The language test asserts `items[0].name_span == None` for every language. It also checks `None` for anonymous Markdown items and for the plain-text root.
  - `provider_name_spans_match_selector_kind_and_item_boundaries` in `src/outline/contents.rs` rejects a name span on an `@hash` anonymous selector and accepts `None` there.
- **The span must be inside the item's own span, on character boundaries.** The same unit test, with source `_é_` and item span (1,3):
  - It accepts the in-item span (1,3).
  - It rejects spans that split the multibyte `é` (1,2) and (3,1).
  - It rejects spans that start before the item (0,3) or end after it (1,4).
  - It rejects `None` for a named selector.

All four tests carry `{test}` markers for the requirement, so there is no marking gap. I found no obligation without a test and no assertion that contradicts the text.
